 import torch
 torch.random.manual_seed(42)
 from torch import nn
 

 dtype = torch.float16
 batch, seq, embed_dim, delay = 2, 16, 4, 2
 x1 = torch.randn(batch, seq, embed_dim, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
 x2 = x1[:, delay:]
 assert torch.allclose(x1[:, delay:], x2)
 net = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim).to("cuda").to(dtype=dtype)
 out1 = net(x1)
 out2 = net(x2)
 print((out1[:, delay:] - out2).abs().max())
 assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)

  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 AssertionError

 Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)

 torch._dynamo.exc.BackendCompilerFailed: backend='inductor' raised:

 This happens both on cpu and cuda devices (A100, 6000 ADA, 2080Ti) and independent of setting dynamic=True/False.

 import torch
 from torch.nested import nested_tensor_from_jagged
 from torch.nn.attention.flex_attention import flex_attention
 

 device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
 H, E_inner, E_value= 8, 16, 32
 lengths_Q = torch.tensor([11, 13, 15])
 lengths_KV = torch.tensor([10, 15, 11])
 offsets_Q = torch.cat([torch.tensor([0]), torch.cumsum(lengths_Q, dim=0)])
 offsets_KV = torch.cat([torch.tensor([0]), torch.cumsum(lengths_KV, dim=0)])
 

 Q = torch.cat([torch.randn(Ni,H,E_inner) for Ni in lengths_Q], dim=0)
 K = torch.cat([torch.randn(Ni,H,E_inner) for Ni in lengths_KV], dim=0)
 V = torch.cat([torch.randn(Ni,H,E_value) for Ni in lengths_KV], dim=0)
 Q = nested_tensor_from_jagged(Q, offsets=offsets_Q )
 K = nested_tensor_from_jagged(K, offsets=offsets_KV)
 V = nested_tensor_from_jagged(V, offsets=offsets_KV)
 Q = Q.moveaxis(1,2).contiguous().to(device) # size=(B, H, j1, E_inner), contiguous=True
 K = K.moveaxis(1,2).contiguous().to(device) # size=(B, H, j2, E_inner), contiguous=True
 V = V.moveaxis(1,2).contiguous().to(device) # size=(B, H, j2, E_value), contiguous=True

 attn_out = flex_attention(Q,K,V) # size=(B, H, j1, E_value), crashes when flex_attention is compiled

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

The benchmark code using `torch.device('mps')` shows ~36 seconds for 100 inferences vs 18 seconds on CPU. Even though Activity Monitor confirms 98.8% GPU utilization, the execution time is about double. This contrasts with CUDA performance on AWS (0.82s) and contradicts the claimed 5x speedup in documentation. I verified this with both nightly builds and source-compiled PyTorch.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
statement: Our current work in SciPy to modernize multivariate distributions requires ensuring compatibility with NumPy's evolving behavior. A key challenge is determining how the 'size' parameter interacts with broadcasting of array-shaped distribution parameters (like 1D/2D arrays). For example, @bashtage's multinomial implementation in a PR demonstrates broadcasting with parameters like n and pvals, where the output shape combines the size parameter, input broadcast dimensions, and variate dimension. We need to understand how to consistently apply this pattern to distributions like multivariate_normal and dirichlet while maintaining alignment with gufunc-style signatures.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.

The 'size' parameter's interaction with array inputs (like 1D/2D parameters) needs careful alignment. A concrete example with the multinomial distribution shows how parameters like n and pvals broadcast to produce output shapes combining (number of samples) × (broadcasted input shape) × (variate dimension). We're seeking clarity on how to generalize this approach to other distributions, such as dirichlet or multivariate_hypergeometric, while preserving gufunc-style signatures.

Thinking a bit more about this, I wonder if URI should statically allow us to register a scheme to behave like a file scheme. Because, we do take an existing well defined URI of scheme file and turn that into vscode-userdata. This in turn means, every client that deals with such a URI would need to ensure that the scheme is converted back to file before using the URI. That seems fragile.

If we could tell URI to treat vscode-userdata like a file scheme, maybe the change would be easier and less fragile?

Turning offexperimentalEditContextEnabled` does fix the behavior, the IME suggestion does not apply to me (AFAICT).
statement: VS Code users with International US keyboards on macOS might face Chinese input issues after using dead keys. Pressing ' then other keys (like ' + space) adds accents correctly, but during editing operations it inserts random ' characters at the cursor. The Chinese input candidate box fails to appear after switching from English, and while disabling `experimentalEditContextEnabled` fixes this, it also disables IME suggestions which aren't relevant to my workflow.
